reader.title: Threatened lynching of Si Beardon
bases: A mob of several hundred surrounded the Springfield jail, threatening to lynch the jailed Black prisoner accused of shooting a policeman, and a second mob a month later led the sheriff to move him to St. Louis (A4, A6, A9, A10).

No one was killed: the mobs surrounded the jail and threatened to lynch Beardon, but the sheriff took him to St. Louis (A4, A9, A10). The episode was a threatened lynching by a crowd of 'several hundred' or '300 men' acting over an accused killing (A4, A6).

The August mob is reported in the Post-Dispatch wire (A2, A4) and in a separately worded brief (A6), and the September move to St. Louis comes from a later St. Louis wire (A9, A10), although the August reports come from one Springfield special and no local paper was found.

summary.text: The threatened lynching of Si Beardon took place at Springfield, Missouri, in August and September 1888, when mobs surrounded the county jail holding Beardon, a Black man accused of shooting a policeman.
No one was lynched, and on September 10 Sheriff Dodson moved Beardon to the St. Louis jail for safekeeping.
Wire reports of his capture and his 'narrow escape' ran in papers from Texas to Washington.
According to a Springfield dispatch, 'Si Burden' shot Policeman Palmer while resisting arrest on Wednesday night, August 8, 1888.
Most reports said the shooting happened on Wednesday, while one Wilmington brief gave Thursday.
The officer was reported as 'fatally wounded', and the September wire said he had been 'murdered'.
At 5 o'clock on the morning of August 10, Marshal Barrett and Officers Snow, Hayes and Dameron found Beardon at the house of Sandy Eslinger, a Black man, eight miles east of Springfield.
By the officers' account, he tried to draw a pistol on Hayes when told to surrender, and Snow fired twice, hitting him in the right breast.
He was taken to jail with a wound expected to kill him within a day or two.
A special to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch reported that the Springfield jail was then 'surrounded by a mob of 300 men who threaten to lynch the desperado'.
A separately worded brief put the crowd at 'several hundred men'.
The Springfield dispatch that named the officers did not mention a mob.
Beardon survived his wounds.

According to a St. Louis dispatch of September 11, a mob surrounded the Springfield jail 'the other night', and Beardon came so close to being lynched that Sheriff Dodson brought him to St. Louis on the night of September 10 and lodged him in jail 'for safe keeping'.
No report of an arrest of anyone in the mobs, of an indictment or of Beardon's trial was found in the coverage.
Only white papers covered the case, mostly in two waves of wire copy.
The August 10 Post-Dispatch special ran on August 11 in Savannah, Richmond, Washington and St. Paul, and a week later in the McCook Tribune.

Its headlines treated the prisoner as guilty and described his wounds with relish: 'Bullets in a Brute's Body', 'A Negro Desperado Shot', and in St. Paul 'The Carcass of a Negro Murderer Perforated with Bullets'.
The McCook paper headed the item 'Dealt With by Judge Lynch', though no lynching had happened.

The September 11 St. Louis wire, headed 'Narrowly Escaped Lynching' in Washington and Memphis and 'Nearly Had Him' in San Antonio, called Beardon 'the negro desperado' and passed over the mob without comment.
Shorter versions appeared in Wilmington, in the German-language Deutsche Correspondent of Baltimore and in Missouri's Chariton Courier.
In these copies the name was printed in many ways, among them Beardon, Bearden, Bearde, Beardle, Bearder, Peardon and Reardon.
The officer was 'Palmer' in the August reports and 'Palmore' or 'Pallmore' in the September wire.
It is also unclear whether the mob of 'the other night' in the September wire was a second crowd or the August 10 one recalled.
The German version placed the mob on the 'vorletzten Nacht', the night before last, which suggests a recent second gathering.

accounts.label: Post-Dispatch special from Springfield (wire)
accounts.gist: Beardon was captured with his body 'filled with lead' and jailed, and a mob of 300 men surrounded the jail threatening to lynch him; he was expected to die.

accounts.label: Springfield dispatch, officers' account
accounts.gist: Marshal Barrett and three officers captured 'Si Burden' at a house east of the city; Officer Snow shot him when he reached for a pistol. It does not mention a mob.

accounts.label: St. Louis wire, September 11
accounts.gist: A mob surrounded the Springfield jail 'the other night' and Beardon had such a narrow escape that Sheriff Dodson brought him to the St. Louis jail.

framing.detail: Papers ran the Post-Dispatch special under headlines that treated the prisoner as guilty and less than human: 'Bullets in a Brute's Body', 'A Negro Desperado Shot', 'Loaded With Lead. The Carcass of a Negro Murderer Perforated with Bullets'.
The September wire reported the near-lynching neutrally, as a 'narrow escape from Judge Lynch', with no comment on the mob.

conflicts.note: The August reports, including the Springfield dispatch, give Palmer; the September St. Louis wire gives Palmore or Pallmore.
Most reports say Wednesday, which the September wire dates August 8; the Wilmington brief alone says Thursday.
No report of Palmer's death itself was found; the September wire calls it murder.
The figures are close and both trace to the August 10 report.

versions.value: August 10, the day he was jailed

conflicts.note: The September wire may describe a second mob or look back at the August one; the German version's 'vorletzten Nacht' (night before last) reads as a recent, second mob (A13).
